Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence at Laodicea on the Lycus (Phrygia; not Laodicea in Syria): Cicero, Pro Flacco 28.68 (speech of 59 BCE) reports that during L. Valerius Flaccus' governorship of Asia (62 BCE) the Jewish gold sent yearly to Jerusalem (Temple tax) was seized after Flaccus' edict forbidding its export: 'at Laodicea a little more than twenty pounds' (by Lucius Peducaeus); c. 100 pounds at Apamea, an unknown amount at Adramyttium, a small amount at Pergamum. Implies an organized Jewish community collecting the Temple tax at Laodicea (probably for its district). Year Established basis: this is the first attestation tied to Laodicea itself. Earlier context (not a row): Josephus Ant. 12.147-153 reports Antiochus III settling 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia/Mesopotamia in Lydia and Phrygia c. 212-205 BCE, but no specific sites are named; some sources (EJ) date the seizure 61-60 BCE and give '20 talents'.

Scholarly estimate based on the Flaccus seizure (62 BCE): Ramsay (Letters to the Seven Churches, 1904, ch. 29) cites Th. Reinach's calculation that the gold seized at Laodicea equalled c. 15,000 silver drachms; at 2 drachms annual tax per man this 'implies a population of 7,500 adult Jewish freemen in the district' (to which women and children must be added). Population left blank: the figure covers the Laodicean district (conventus), not the city alone, and counts only adult men. Ramsay also notes no Jewish inscription of Laodicea itself survives and Jews there are known from Josephus Ant. 14.10.20.

Trebilco (Durham PhD thesis 1987, ch. 1 section 5.2.2) on the Flaccus seizure of 62 BCE (a little more than twenty pounds of gold at Laodicea): the four cities were each centres of a regional conventus, so the sums were probably the total tax of several communities and likely of several years (held back owing to disturbed conditions), sometimes with extra gifts; 'it remains impossible to estimate the actual population of the Jewish communities of the four areas involved' though large Jewish populations were involved. Population blank (no estimate for the city). He also notes the 2,000 Jewish families settled in Lydia and Phrygia by Antiochus III (212-205/4 BCE; probably over 10,000 people) were spread over unspecified sites, so no single settlement can be sized.

Letter of the magistrates of Laodicea to the Roman proconsul Gaius Rabirius (Josephus, Ant. 14.241-243): an envoy of the high priest Hyrcanus (II) delivered the proconsul's letter, and the Laodiceans agreed that the Jews may observe their Sabbaths and other rites according to their ancestral laws; documents an organized Jewish community at Laodicea whose privileges were upheld. Date c. 45 BCE (Juster; c. = approximate); Saulnier dates it 48/47 BCE; Trebilco notes it could instead refer to Hyrcanus I (late 2nd c. BCE).

Event: earthquake destroyed the city of Laodicea, which was soon rebuilt (Jewish Encyclopedia gives the year 62; Tacitus, Annals 14.27, places the earthquake in 60 CE). The same article notes Jews lived at Laodicea (Antiochus III's transfer of 2,000 families to Phrygia; Flaccus' confiscation of more than twenty pounds of Temple gold contributed by the Jews of Laodicea). Effect on the Jewish community not documented; Population blank.
